title: Finding Unstated Warrants
short: State the general principle an argument takes for granted, then ask whether the audience would accept it.
trouble: Learners restate the claim and call it the warrant.

blocks.html: In the Toulmin model, the warrant links grounds to claim. Writers often leave it unstated because it seems obvious to them. Your job, as a reader and as a writer, is to say it out loud and then ask: would this audience accept it?

blocks.text: Three steps to find a warrant

items: Find the claim and the grounds.
Write a general sentence that would make the grounds count as a reason for the claim: “In general, if [grounds], then [claim].”
Test it: is it true in general? Would your audience agree? Are there exceptions (which become rebuttals)?

blocks.html: A warrant is the general principle an argument takes for granted. State it plainly, then ask whether the audience would accept it. If they wouldn’t, the argument needs backing for its warrant, not more grounds.

An argument can have perfect evidence and still fail because its warrant is weak or unshared. If you never state your warrant, you can’t defend it, and a skeptical reader will quietly reject your whole argument without telling you why.

blocks.title: Find the warrant
blocks.q: “Ms. Lee has taught for thirty years, so her advice about study habits is worth following.”
steps: Claim: her advice about study habits is worth following. Grounds: she has taught for thirty years.
Warrant: long experience teaching gives a person good insight into how students learn.
Test: most readers would accept it, with a qualifier: experience usually helps, though it doesn’t guarantee every piece of advice is right.
blocks.a: Warrant: long teaching experience gives insight into how students learn.

blocks.title: A warrant the audience may reject
blocks.q: “Three towns near us built splash pads, so our town should build one too.”
steps: Grounds: three nearby towns built splash pads. Claim: our town should build one.
Warrant: what neighboring towns build, we should build.

Test: a careful reader may reject that. Other towns may have more money or more young families. The writer needs a better warrant, such as “a splash pad serves families with young children, and our town has many,” with grounds to match.
blocks.a: The warrant (“do what other towns do”) is weak; the argument needs a better one.

blocks.html: Restating the claim and calling it the warrant. For “The park needs more benches because older walkers have nowhere to rest,” the warrant is not “The park needs benches.” It is the general principle: a park should meet the needs of the people who use it. Check: a warrant mentions neither this park nor these benches; it would apply to other cases too.

blocks.name: wr-toulmin

opts.claim: The park should add benches along the walking path.
opts.grounds: Many older walkers stop and rest on the low wall by the pond.
opts.warrant: A park should meet the needs of the people who use it.

blocks.cap: Label the claim, the grounds and the warrant, then Check.
